roles: Tanna (rabbinic sage of the Mishnaic period)
traditionally counted a martyr (of the Ten Martyrs)
summary: Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef (c. 50-135 CE) was one of the foremost of the Tannaim, the rabbinic sages of Roman Palestine, and a foundational figure of rabbinic Judaism. The tradition remembers him as a shepherd who began the study of Torah late in life and rose to be the master of his generation, as the organizer of the accumulated legal traditions into the topical arrangement that underlies the later redaction of the Mishnah, as the developer of a maximalist hermeneutic that finds meaning in every particle of the Torah, as a supporter of the Bar Kokhba revolt against Rome, and, in the Talmud's account, as a martyr executed by the Romans who died reciting the Shema.
description:
Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef, one of the greatest of the Tannaim, was a leading rabbinic sage of Roman Palestine in the late first and early second centuries CE, conventionally dated c. 50-135 CE. In the tradition's own account of him he was of humble origin, a shepherd who came to the study of Torah only as an adult, and who nonetheless became the master of his generation and the teacher from whose school much of the classical rabbinic tradition descends (Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, and others are remembered as his disciples). The biographical details preserved in the rabbinic sources are transmitted as aggadah, the tradition's narrative lore, and the modern scholarship (Louis Finkelstein; Barry Holtz) reads them as such, as a shaped rabbinic portrait rather than as documentary biography, while the figure himself is firmly attested across the tannaitic corpus.

In the history of the law Akiva is associated above all with the organization of the oral tradition. The rabbinic memory and the standard scholarly reconstruction credit him with gathering and arranging the accumulated legal traditions by subject, the arrangement that his disciples transmitted and that stands behind the redaction of the Mishnah by Judah ha-Nasi around 200 CE; the Talmud pictures an anonymous or undesignated mishnah as following the opinion of Rabbi Akiva. He is also remembered for a distinctive, maximalist method of scriptural interpretation, in which every particle of the Torah, down to particles such as et, is held to carry teachable meaning, a method the tradition contrasts with the more restrained hermeneutic of his contemporary Rabbi Ishmael. His exegetical school is associated with the tannaitic midrashim (the Sifra on Leviticus and the Sifrei that follow his method), and the halakhic midrashim of the school of Akiva are a principal witness to his interpretive approach.

Akiva's ethical and theological teaching is preserved in the open primary corpus. In tractate Avot a saying is recorded in his name that 'Beloved is man, for he was created in the image [of God]; especially beloved is he for it was made known to him that he had been created in the image [of God], as it is said: for in the image of God He made man (Genesis 9:6)' (Pirkei Avot 3:14, read on Sefaria). And in the tannaitic tradition, transmitted in the Sifra and the Jerusalem Talmud, Akiva is the sage who names the great organizing principle of the Torah: on the verse 'you shall love your neighbor as yourself' (Leviticus 19:18), 'Rabbi Akiva says: this is a great principle in the Torah', with Ben Azzai offering the verse on the common descent of humankind (Genesis 5:1) as a yet greater principle (Sifra, Kedoshim 4:12; Jerusalem Talmud, Nedarim 9:4, both read on Sefaria).

Akiva supported the revolt of Bar Kokhba against Rome (132-135 CE), and in the aggadah he is reported to have hailed Bar Kokhba as the messiah, applying to him the verse 'a star (kokhav) shall come out of Jacob' (Numbers 24:17), a messianic acclamation recorded in the Jerusalem Talmud and set here as the traditional/aggadic account, attributed and not adjudicated. After the failure of the revolt he was, in the Talmud's narrative, arrested by the Romans for teaching Torah in defiance of a decree and put to death. The Babylonian Talmud gives the martyrdom at length (Berakhot 61b, read on Sefaria): as they took him out to be executed it was the time for the recitation of the Shema, and while the Romans raked his flesh with iron combs he recited it, accepting upon himself the yoke of Heaven; to his students' astonishment he explained, 'All my days I have been troubled by the verse: With all your soul (Deuteronomy 6:5), meaning: even if God takes your soul. I said to myself: when will the opportunity be afforded me to fulfill this? Now that it has been afforded me, shall I not fulfill it?', and 'he prolonged his uttering of the word One until his soul left his body as he uttered his final word: One.' This martyrdom narrative is presented here as the Talmud's own account, on the tradition's terms, with the note that the scholarship treats the martyrologies as shaped rabbinic literature. In the later tradition Akiva is numbered among the Ten Martyrs commemorated in the liturgy.
editorial_notes: This entry presents Rabbi Akiva on Judaism's own terms (neutrality #1, #4, #6), as the tradition remembers and honours him, its foremost Tanna, organizer of the oral law behind the Mishnah, author of a maximalist hermeneutic, and martyr. Several load-bearing items are handled as attributed accounts, not as documented biography, per neutrality #1-#2: (a) the biographical portrait (the late-starting shepherd who became the master of his generation) is transmitted as aggadah and read as shaped rabbinic narrative in the scholarship (Finkelstein; Holtz), and is so labelled; (b) Akiva's support of the Bar Kokhba revolt and, in particular, the messianic acclamation of Bar Kokhba (applying Numbers 24:17, 'a star shall come out of Jacob') are given as the aggadic/traditional account (Jerusalem Talmud), attributed and not adjudicated, with mashiach linked as the relevant concept; (c) the martyrdom is given as the Babylonian Talmud's own account (Berakhot 61b), with a note that the martyrologies are studied as rabbinic literature. Three primary passages were READ line-by-line on open Sefaria and are rated high, carrying the load-bearing claims: Berakhot 61b (the martyrdom, Akiva's gloss on 'with all your soul' as 'even if God takes your soul', the recitation of the Shema under torture, and his death prolonging the word 'One'), quoted verbatim; Pirkei Avot 3:14 (the 'beloved is man, created in the image of God' saying, quoted verbatim; the speaker is Akiva, the immediately preceding mishnah 3:13 opening 'Rabbi Akiva said' and 3:14 continuing 'He used to say'); and the 'great principle' teaching on Leviticus 19:18, read verbatim in both the Sifra (Kedoshim 4:12) and the Jerusalem Talmud (Nedarim 9:4), where 'Rabbi Akiva says: this is a great principle in the Torah'. Sources triangulate the three lenses per neutrality #8-9: (a) academic historians of the Tannaim (Louis Finkelstein, Akiba: Scholar, Saint and Martyr; Barry Holtz, Rabbi Akiva: Sage of the Talmud, which explicitly reads the Akiva stories as rabbinic literature; Strack and Stemberger for the halakhic midrashim of the school of Akiva); (b) the open primary texts on Sefaria (Berakhot 61b, Pirkei Avot 3:14, Sifra Kedoshim 4:12, and Jerusalem Talmud Nedarim 9:4), READ line-by-line and quoted, rated high; (c) contemporary Jewish scholars (Holtz). No encyclopedias, no Wikipedia, no tertiary sources. Confidence: the four open Sefaria primary passages are high (read line-by-line and quoted); Finkelstein, Holtz, and Strack-Stemberger are medium (verified to exist and be on-topic via publisher and library records, not read line-by-line). Finkelstein's 1936 biography is cited with its original publisher (Covici, Friede, New York), not JPS. Dating (c. 50-135 CE) is conventional and approximate in the scholarship. Relation targets shimon-bar-yochai, judah-ha-nasi, mishnah, talmud, oral-torah, rabbinic-judaism, halakha, tanakh, shema, and mashiach all exist; aggadah is authored in the same batch (Akiva's own biography and the Bar Kokhba acclamation are transmitted as aggadah). The reciprocal student_of from shimon-bar-yochai to rabbi-akiva is already recorded there and is now satisfied by this file.

lifespan.note: c. 50-135 CE; the years are conventional and approximate in the scholarship. His death is placed in the aftermath of the Bar Kokhba revolt (132-135 CE), and the tradition remembers him as executed by the Romans; the precise date is not established.

relations.note: The rabbinic tradition remembers Shimon bar Yochai (Rashbi) as a leading disciple of Rabbi Akiva; much of Rashbi's transmission stands in the line of Akiva's teaching. The shimon-bar-yochai entry exists and records the reciprocal student_of relation.

Judah ha-Nasi's redaction of the Mishnah (c. 200 CE) rests on the earlier topical organization of the oral law that the tradition and the standard scholarship associate with Rabbi Akiva and his disciples; the Talmud pictures an undesignated mishnah as following Akiva's opinion. The judah-ha-nasi entry exists.
As one of the foremost of the Tannaim, whose school and disciples shaped the classical rabbinic tradition, Rabbi Akiva is a central figure of the rabbinic movement. The rabbinic-judaism entry exists.

Rabbi Akiva is associated in the tradition and the scholarship with the topical organization of the oral law (Torah she-be-al peh), the arrangement his disciples transmitted and that underlies the Mishnah. The oral-torah entry exists.

The organization of the accumulated legal traditions credited to Akiva and his disciples stands behind Judah ha-Nasi's redaction of the Mishnah; the Talmud treats an undesignated mishnah as following Akiva's view. The mishnah entry exists.

The Babylonian Talmud preserves the extended narrative of Akiva's arrest and martyrdom (Berakhot 61b), read line-by-line for this entry on open Sefaria; teachings in his name are transmitted throughout the Talmud. The talmud entry exists.

Akiva's maximalist hermeneutic (finding teachable meaning in every particle of the Torah) and the halakhic midrashim of his school (the Sifra and the Sifrei that follow his method) are a principal foundation of the derivation of halakha. The halakha entry exists.

In the Talmud's martyrdom account (Berakhot 61b), Akiva is executed while reciting the Shema, dying as he prolongs the word 'One'; his gloss on 'with all your soul' (Deuteronomy 6:5) as 'even if God takes your soul' is read line-by-line for this entry. The shema entry exists.

Akiva's distinctive maximalist exegesis takes the text of the Torah (within the Tanakh) as bearing meaning in its every particle; his teachings turn throughout on the interpretation of scriptural verses. The tanakh entry exists.

In the aggadah (Jerusalem Talmud), Akiva is reported to have hailed Bar Kokhba, leader of the revolt against Rome (132-135 CE), as the messiah (mashiach), applying to him the verse 'a star shall come out of Jacob' (Numbers 24:17). This is recorded as the traditional/aggadic account, attributed and not adjudicated. The mashiach entry exists.

He prolonged his uttering of the word One until his soul left his body as he uttered his final word: One.' Read line-by-line and quoted verbatim from Sefaria.

sources.citation: Finkelstein, Louis. Akiba: Scholar, Saint and Martyr. New York: Covici, Friede, 1936 (repr. Jewish Publication Society and others). The classic scholarly biography of Rabbi Akiva by a leading scholar of rabbinic Judaism; cited for Akiva's place among the Tannaim, his role in the organization of the oral law, and the traditional biographical portrait, which it reconstructs from the rabbinic sources. Verified to exist and be on-topic (author, title, and original publisher confirmed via library records and Internet Archive); not read line-by-line.
sources.license: Older scholarly monograph; cited for reference (Internet Archive scan of the 1936 edition).

sources.citation: Holtz, Barry W. Rabbi Akiva: Sage of the Talmud. Jewish Lives. New Haven: Yale University Press, 2017. A contemporary scholarly biography that draws on recent scholarship on rabbinic narrative to present Akiva's life, reading the Akiva stories (his late start in study, his teaching, his martyrdom) as shaped rabbinic literature rather than documentary biography; cited as the contemporary Jewish scholarly lens and for the literary character of the Akiva traditions. Verified to exist and be on-topic (Yale University Press record, ISBN 9780300204872); not read line-by-line.

Strack, H. L., and Gunter Stemberger. Introduction to the Talmud and Midrash. Trans. and ed. Markus Bockmuehl. 2nd English ed., Minneapolis: Fortress Press, 1996. The standard one-volume critical introduction to rabbinic literature; cited for the halakhic midrashim of the school of Rabbi Akiva (the Sifra and the Sifrei that follow his hermeneutic) and for the tannaitic period within which Akiva worked, carrying the same medium rating it holds in judah-ha-nasi.json.
